title: Non-blocking follow-up from backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups's PR #364 review
description: Non-blocking finding from pr-reviewer's PR #364 review of backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups. PR #364 was accepted (full test suite 1491 passed/100% coverage reproduced, ruff/mypy clean, code-review skill pass clean, and the concurrency + defensive-path mutation-testing claims independently reproduced by hand-reverting the code and confirming each of the sampled tests genuinely fails, then restoring). This is the one item worth tracking so it isn't lost once the PR merges.

checklist.step: GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis's own concurrent daily/weekly/extended-data fetch (app/api/routers/stocks.py get_analysis, ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3)) now has its 'extended' leg call into get_extended_data, which PR #364 made concurrent in its own right (a second, nested ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) in app/data/yfinance_provider.py). One GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis request can therefore transiently spin up up to 6 worker threads (3 outer + 3 inner, only while the extended leg is in flight) instead of 3 -- not a correctness bug (the two pools are independent, no shared state or ordering between them, no deadlock risk), but it compounds with the already-tracked per-leg DB-connection-pool footprint finding (docs/tasks/backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups.json's checklist item 5 / this same PR's decisions entry reconfirming it). Worth reconsidering together with that finding if either this per-call-nested-pool pattern spreads to more endpoints, or real usage ever approaches concurrency levels where total thread/connection fan-out (not just the DB pool specifically) becomes a real resource concern.

decisions.decision: No code change: reconfirmed that get_analysis's transient up-to-6-worker-thread footprint (its own outer ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) for daily/weekly/extended, plus get_extended_data's independent inner ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) for calendar/info/insider_transactions while the extended leg is in flight) is acceptable headroom and does not need tuning or restructuring.
decisions.rationale: Worked the actual thread/resource math rather than guessing. (1) Peak concurrency per /analysis request is 6 OS threads, not more: get_analysis's 3 outer futures all start immediately (max_workers == futures submitted), and only the one running the extended leg blocks on get_extended_data's own 3 inner futures -- so the ceiling is 2 idle-but-alive outer threads (daily/weekly, likely already finishing since they're single-property-equivalent fetches) + 1 blocked outer thread + 3 inner threads = 6, for at most the extended leg's own worst-case duration (bounded by _REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=10s per _clamp_session_timeout, same budget the inner pool was already designed to close down from ~30s worst case in the parent followups task). (2) 6 is not an outlier against this codebase's own existing precedent: two sibling per-request fan-outs already run more workers than this -- day_trader_signal.py's _fan_out_per_ticker and portfolio/pricing.py's enrich_positions_with_price both use max_workers=8 (_MAX_CONCURRENT_TICKER_FETCHES/_MAX_CONCURRENT_PRICE_FETCHES) -- and Python's own ThreadPoolExecutor default sizing when max_workers is left unset (min(32, (os.cpu_count() or 1) + 4)) is itself far above 6 on any machine with more than 2 cores (28 on this dev container's own 24-core host). (3) OS threads are cheap relative to the resource this same review thread already flagged as the real constraint: backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups's checklist item 5 empirically load-tested get_analysis's actual scarce resource -- its SQLAlchemy QueuePool DB connections (pool_size=5/max_overflow=10=15 total, backend/app/db/session.py) -- at 10-12 concurrent requests (30-36 simultaneous connection demands) with graceful queuing and no OperationalError/pool TimeoutError; that finding already covers the concurrency regime where this endpoint's fan-out would actually start to hurt, and nothing about this checklist item's nested-thread-pool shape changes that DB-connection math (get_extended_data's inner pool opens no DB session of its own -- it only reads yfinance Ticker properties against the process-wide YfData session singleton). A bare thread, by contrast, has no equivalent hard cap or shared-resource contention in this app to exhaust. Considered and rejected two concrete code changes: (a) reducing get_extended_data's own max_workers when it's known to be called from inside get_analysis's fan-out -- rejected because get_extended_data has no way to know its calling context without an intrusive extra parameter threaded through DataProvider's protocol, purely to save at most 2-3 transient threads for a few seconds, which the math above shows isn't a real constraint; (b) collapsing the outer/inner pools into one shared executor -- rejected for the same reason backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups's decisions entry already gave for not consolidating get_analysis's fail-fast/scoped-session shape with get_indicator_history's/pricing.py's/day_trader_signal.py's full-wait shape: get_extended_data's own fail-fast semantics (manual shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True), no per-leg DB session to race) are independently justified and specific to that call site, and forcing it to share get_analysis's pool would reintroduce exactly the kind of cross-cutting coupling that task explicitly avoided. Verified no regression risk from this no-code-change confirmation by re-running the two relevant test files unmodified (tests/unit/data/test_yfinance_provider.py, tests/integration/test_stocks_analysis.py: 69 passed). Worth reconsidering only if a third level of nested per-request fan-out is ever added on top of these two, or if real usage approaches the DB-connection-pool concurrency regime the parent task's own load test already identified as the actual limit.
